We like a budget that makes the accountant nod before the minister starts smiling.

We oppose this approach to wealth and taxation. Less public revenue leaves a question about who helps a household without substantial savings when their private budget is no longer enough. That reflects our commitment to resources shared according to need rather than wealth when judging wealth and taxation. Even though a useful service need not make a complete personal record the price of participation, it does not answer our concern about the economic balance. We think a billionaire can survive a tax bill without a national day of mourning.

We oppose this proposal on wealth and taxation because we value political unity rather than a permanent right to obstruct: a stronger private boundary can also make a public duty harder to enforce. The economic case—a household without substantial savings keeps more room to decide what matters in their own budget instead of surrendering that choice to government—does not remove our objection about power in wealth and taxation. Nothing ruins decisive leadership like having to ask the people’s representatives for permission.
c: You can live with this combination on wealth and taxation: a household without substantial savings keeps more room to decide what matters in their own budget instead of surrendering that choice to government, while you can also accept the aim to leave people more control over private information and personal boundaries.
